title: Architecture Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADR Process
author: Priya Desai
body:
Overview

Purpose:
This page consolidates Redwood Inference's architecture and engineering standards across API design, coding, infrastructure (IaC), model-serving, observability, and performance. It also documents the ADR (Architecture Decision Record) process and links to representative ADRs. The goal is to provide a single reference for teams building services and model-serving integrations on the Redwood platform.

Scope:
Applies to all Redwood-hosted services, Dedicated and Private control-plane components, runtime components of the serving engine, and customer-facing APIs. For team-level deviations, follow the ADR process described below.

Ownership and Contacts:
- Standards owner: Architecture & Standards guild (architecture-and-standards@redwood.example.com)
- Primary contact: Priya Desai (author)
- Reviewers: Marcus Lee (Servings Runtime), Elena Rodriguez (Eng Platform)

Principles (high level):
1. Stability-first: backward compatible changes preferred; clearly communicated breaking changes via versioning and deprecation windows.
2. Observable-by-default: all services must emit structured logs, traces, and metrics for critical flows.
3. Production economics: prioritize designs that reduce token/unit cost while preserving SLOs.
4. Security and privacy by design: default to least privilege, encryption in transit and at rest, and restrict sensitive data flows.
5. Developer ergonomics: consistent patterns, linting, and templates to speed onboarding.

1) API Standards
- Naming and resource structure:
  - Use plural nouns: /v1/models, /v1/encodings, /v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/routes
  - Keep verbs in operations only for RPC-like actions: /v1/models/{id}:retrain
- Versioning:
  - All public APIs are versioned in the base path (e.g., /v1, /v2).
  - Major versions may contain breaking changes; minor releases are additive.
  - Deprecation policy: announce 90 days prior and maintain backward compatibility where reasonable.
- Authentication & Authorization:
  - Bearer tokens (short-lived) for user-level API access; mutual TLS for control-plane-to-control-plane.
  - Scopes: tokens should carry scope claims (read:models, write:routes, admin).
- Request/Response patterns:
  - Use JSON for control-plane APIs. Streaming generation APIs use chunked transfer and newline-delimited JSON for events.
  - Responses should include request_id, processing_time_ms, and model_metadata where applicable.
- Error Handling:
  - Use structured error envelopes: {"error": {"code": "RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED", "message": "...", "request_id": "..."}}
  - HTTP mapping: 4xx for client errors, 429 for rate limits, 5xx for server issues.
- Rate limiting and quotas:
  - Default per-API tier rate limits: Free: 60 req/min, Pro: 600 req/min, Enterprise: configurable.
  - Token-level throttling for generation endpoints with per-model capacity tokens.
- Example: Generation request:
  POST /v1/generate
  Headers: Authorization: Bearer <token>
  Body:
  {
    "model": "redwood-rlm-1.2",
    "input": "Summarize the following...",
    "max_tokens": 512,
    "stream": true
  }

2) Coding Standards
- Languages and frameworks:
  - Control-plane services: Go (1.20+) or TypeScript (Node 20+) depending on service characteristics.
  - Serving/runtime components: C++ for kernels, Rust/Go for performance-sensitive orchestration, Python for orchestration glue tests only.
- Formatting and linting:
  - Go: gofmt + golangci-lint with enabled checks: govet, staticcheck, ineffassign.
  - TypeScript: Prettier + ESLint (recommended config: airbnb-base plus Redwood overrides).
- Testing:
  - Unit tests: target >= 90% coverage for critical libraries, >= 70% for application code.
  - Integration tests: run in CI against a local-integration environment that includes the model-serving runtime mock.
  - Performance/regression tests: all changes to serving runtime or API path must include benchmark results and a performance ticket when regressions exceed thresholds.
- Pull Request process:
  - PRs require at least one approver from owning team and passing CI.
  - Large or risky changes require design doc link in PR and at least two reviewer approvals.
- Dependency policy:
  - Use approved dependencies list. High-risk native modules or BLAS/kernels must be reviewed by the runtime team.

3) Infrastructure (IaC) Standards
- Tooling and structure:
  - Use Terraform for multi-cloud infra and Terragrunt for environment composition.
  - Micro-modules for reuse: network, iam, compute, gpu-pool, k8s-cluster, rds, s3-bucket.
- Environment separation:
  - Environments: dev, staging, prod. Network isolation between prod and non-prod.
  - Naming convention: <team>-<env>-<resource-type>-<short> (e.g., serving-prod-gpu-01).
- Networking and security:
  - Private subnets for control-plane, public-facing API endpoints in a dedicated ALB with WAF.
  - VPC peering and Transit Gateway patterns for Private deployments.
  - KMS for all secrets; HSM for enterprise key material when requested.
- Observability and access:
  - Centralized CloudWatch/Datadog metrics ingestion; apply standard tags: team, service, env, owner.
- Terraform CI/CD:
  - All infra changes must go through PR and apply via an automated pipeline. Approvals required for prod changes.

4) Model-serving Standards
- Packaging and model catalog:
  - Models must be registered in the internal model catalog with metadata: model_id, architecture, tokenizer, quantization profile, benchmark profile, owner, governance notes.
- Model variants and compatibility:
  - Each model in the catalog should have at least one CPU and one GPU-compatible variant when feasible, and a quantized variant (int8/4-bit) with verified quality metrics.
- KV cache and prefix caching:
  - Runtime should expose configuration knobs for KV cache TTL, max entries, and eviction policy per-model. Default TTL: 300s for conversational sessions.
- Batching and concurrency:
  - Default continuous batching enabled for all GPU-backed backends. Batching config must include max_batch_size and max_latency_ms. Typical defaults for generation workloads: max_batch_size=32, max_latency_ms=50.
- Quantization and kernels:
  - Quantization profiles maintained in confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles. Automated validation with a standard eval harness (applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness).
  - Kernel selection is done by the runtime based on model architecture and hardware; teams may provide kernel hints via model metadata.
- Fallbacks and graceful degradation:
  - Routing policy must declare fallbacks: cheaper-variant, lower-precision, or cross-region routing. Fallthrough order example: redwood-rlm-2.0-quant -> redwood-rlm-2.0-fp16 -> redwood-rlm-1.8.
- Security and data handling:
  - No PII persisted in control-plane logs; customer-provided prompts are redacted per privacy policy. For enterprise Private deployments, customers must configure retention and redaction settings.

5) Observability Standards
- Metrics:
  - Emit service-level and model-level metrics: request_count, request_latency_ms (p50/p90/p99), token_count, batch_size_histogram, model_load_time_ms, kv_cache_hit_rate.
  - Metric naming convention: redwood.<service>.<metric> (e.g., redwood.inference.request_count).
- Traces:
  - Use OpenTelemetry for distributed tracing. Every API entry point must attach a trace id. Span naming: <service>.<operation>.
  - Capture key attributes: model_id, model_variant, request_size_tokens, tenant_id (obfuscated for PII).
- Logs:
  - Structured JSON logs with keys: timestamp, level, service, env, request_id, msg, err?.
  - Sampling: debug logs sampled at 0.1% in prod by default; critical errors never sampled out.
- Dashboards and alerts:
  - Standard dashboards: Service overview, Model performance (latency, tokens, cost), SLO health, Error taxonomy.
  - Alerts: page on SLO burn rate >2x projected or p99 latency > SLO for 10 minutes. Use PagerDuty escalation policies.

6) Performance Standards and Benchmarks
- SLO definitions (example):
  - API control-plane: availability 99.95% monthly, p95 latency < 150ms for metadata and config endpoints.
  - Inference generation endpoints (hosted): availability 99.9% monthly, p50 latency < 50ms (short prompts, <128 tokens), p90 < 200ms, p99 < 800ms.
  - Dedicated GPU pools: throughput SLAs in tokens/sec per GPU and tail-latency guarantees based on committed capacity.
- Benchmarking requirements:
  - New models or runtime kernels must be benchmarked under representative workloads (mix of short chat, long-completion, embedding). Provide a benchmark report: hardware, model variant, batch config, throughput (tokens/sec), latencies (p50/p90/p99), memory footprint, and cost estimate.
- Performance regression process:
  - Any change resulting in >5% regression in p90 latency or >3% regression in throughput requires blocking CI job and a rollback plan.

7) ADR (Architecture Decision Record) Process
- When to create an ADR:
  - Non-trivial architectural choices, breaking API changes, infra patterns, or changes to model-serving runtime knobs.
- ADR template (minimum fields):
  1) Title
  2) Status (proposed | accepted | superseded | deprecated)
  3) Context (problem statement)
  4) Decision (what, why)
  5) Consequences (operational, cost, compatibility)
  6) Owners and reviewers
  7) Date
- ADR lifecycle:
  - Draft ADRs reviewed by the Architecture & Standards guild. After approval, status moves to accepted and the ADR is linked from the relevant standards pages. Superseded ADRs must reference the new ADR.
- Example ADR summary (short):
  - ADR-2026-01: "Model Quantization Defaults"
    - Status: accepted
    - Decision: Default model shipping uses int8 quantized variants where eval delta <= 1% absolute on key eval sets.
    - Consequences: Reduced memory and cost; must run validation harness prior to enabling for production.

Operational runbooks and rollout guidance:
- Rolling changes to runtime:
  1) Create a canary deployment (small percentage of traffic) with feature flags and telemetry hooks.
  2) Monitor SLOs (latency, error rate) and model-quality evals on canary traffic for 24 hours.
  3) If no regressions, perform staged rollout to 25% / 50% / 100% over configurable windows.
  4) Automatic rollback if p99 latency increases by >25% or error rate > 0.5% absolute from baseline.

Audit and compliance notes:
- All ADRs, model-catalog entries, and infra changes must be retained with audit logs for 12 months by default. Higher retention for customer-specific Private deployments can be configured through the compliance package.

Appendix: Example Terraform module header (narrative table)
- Network module inputs:
  - name (string) - resource name prefix
  - cidr_block (string) - VPC CIDR
  - environment (string) - dev|staging|prod
  - owners (list) - team owners
- Example usage snippet:
  terraform apply -var-file=prod.tfvars -auto-approve

Related action items:
- Teams must validate impacted services against these standards within 60 days of publication and open any compliance exceptions as tickets in the Architecture & Standards board.

If you have questions or need an exception, contact architecture-and-standards@redwood.example.com or open a ticket and propose an ADR.
